The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on the traffic signals maintained by transportation departments.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Flock does not sell</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cameras</strong></td> <td>Commercial, doorbell, body, dash, and phone cameras already cover most public space</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access to footage</strong></td> <td>Victims and bystanders supply footage directly, and phone video spreads online</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License plate readers</strong></td> <td>The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on traffic signals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The scarce thing is the database.</strong> Flock aggregates plate reads, locations, and timestamps into a searchable record of movement, then sells access to it. The pitch to departments comes down to one line worth remembering: the same information a warrant would produce, but with no warrant and no wait.</p> <hr> <h2 id="a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction"> <a href="#a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction" title="A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction">A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction</a> <a href="#a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction">#</a> </h2> <p>Phone carriers, car makers, and phone vendors each hold large location stores. Those stores carry legal friction. A request for one person’s movement history needs a warrant, and a warrant needs probable cause, a judge, and a written record. Courts have repeatedly narrowed the broad geo-fence warrants after challenges.</p> <p>Flock sells an equivalent record without the friction. Its stated position is simple: movement on public roads is public, so no warrant applies.</p> <p>The asymmetry is the whole business. The same movement data costs a warrant when a carrier holds it and nothing when Flock holds it. Removing the warrant removes the record of the search, and the record of the search is the part the public audits.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-fourth-amendment"> <a href="#the-fourth-amendment" title="The Fourth Amendment">The Fourth Amendment</a> <a href="#the-fourth-amendment" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Fourth Amendment">#</a> </h2> <p>The amendment reads as a defense against general searches. Its full text:</p> <blockquote> <p>The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.</p> </blockquote> <p>The amendment responds to the general warrants, called writs of assistance, in use before independence. Those writs named no specific place or person and carried no expiry. Officials searched anywhere, at any time, on vague suspicion. The amendment rejects the practice by tying every search to probable cause, a sworn statement, and a particular description.</p> <p>Flock’s service removes all three in one step: no probable cause, no oath, no particular description. The video’s point is blunt. A subscription dispensing with the warrant dispenses with the entire safeguard.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-case-law"> <a href="#the-case-law" title="The Case Law">The Case Law</a> <a href="#the-case-law" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Case Law">#</a> </h2> <p>Two lines of authority collide here.</p> <p>The older line holds recording what happens on a public road needs no warrant, because a person on a public road keeps no reasonable expectation of privacy in the movements seen there. Flock leans on this line and the 1984 case the video discusses.</p> <p>The newer line pulls the other way. <strong>United States v. Jones</strong> (2012) held a GPS tracker fixed to a vehicle, and followed for weeks, is a search needing a warrant even on public roads. <strong>Carpenter v. United States</strong> (2018) reached the same result for cell-site location records held by wireless carriers, because a person keeps a reasonable expectation of privacy in the record of their physical movements.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Case</th> <th>Year</th> <th>Result</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Public-recording line</strong></td> <td>1984</td> <td>Recording movement from a public corner needs no warrant, since an officer present sees the same thing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>United States v. Jones</strong></td> <td>2012</td> <td>A GPS device tracking a car over a sustained period needs a warrant, even on public roads</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Carpenter v. United States</strong></td> <td>2018</td> <td>Cell-site location records need a warrant, since a person keeps privacy in the record of their movements</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Chhatri v. United States</strong></td> <td>cited in the video</td> <td>Location shared with a third party stays protected, so the warrant requirement survives</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Flock’s product is the comprehensive movement record Jones and Carpenter protect. The company argues its cameras escape those rulings because a sensor, not a GPS unit or a cell tower, gathers the positions. The distinction is in the sensor, not in the underlying record.</em></p> <p><strong>Legal boundary:</strong> Jones and Carpenter do not decide every automated license-plate-reader dispute. The cases provide a constitutional framework for long-term location tracking and government access to movement records. Courts, statutory rules, retention periods, access controls, and the facts of a particular query still affect the result. The sales claims in this article are an argument for scrutiny, not a substitute for jurisdiction-specific legal advice.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-loophole-in-their-own-words"> <a href="#the-loophole-in-their-own-words" title="The Loophole in Their Own Words">The Loophole in Their Own Words</a> <a href="#the-loophole-in-their-own-words" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Loophole in Their Own Words">#</a> </h2> <p>A series of word choices does the legal work. Each one rewrites the same product out of the reach of the cases above.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Sells access, not the record.</strong> Flock states it sells a subscription to query the database, so it sells no comprehensive record of movement.</li> <li><strong>Shares derived data, not your data.</strong> The wording restyles every plate read, timestamp, and route as mined material, so no raw personal data changes hands.</li> <li><strong>Queried, not searched.</strong> The Fourth Amendment stops unreasonable searches, and Flock frames every lookup as a query, so no search occurs.</li> </ul> <p><em>Each phrase relabels the same act. The activity stays identical to the thing a warrant would guard. Only the noun changes.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="two-contradictory-pitches"> <a href="#two-contradictory-pitches" title="Two Contradictory Pitches">Two Contradictory Pitches</a> <a href="#two-contradictory-pitches" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Contradictory Pitches">#</a> </h2> <p>Flock sells the same service two ways at once, and the versions contradict each other.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Audience</th> <th>The pitch</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Law enforcement</strong></td> <td>Wide, deep, and fast search, no delays, no warrants</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>The public and commissioners</strong></td> <td>Small, limited, safe, slow, and cautious, tied to lower crime</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The statements conflict. A database searched wide, deep, and fast with no warrants is not small or cautious in any sense the public hears. The one clause both sides share is a promise of lower crime, and the promise carries the sale. Many commissioners voting for cameras hold this belief honestly and never see the tool as mass surveillance.</p> <hr> <h2 id="what-the-records-show"> <a href="#what-the-records-show" title="What the Records Show">What the Records Show</a> <a href="#what-the-records-show" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Records Show">#</a> </h2> <p>Concrete examples sharpen the concern beyond prediction.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Pflugerville, Texas.</strong> A town of roughly 70,000 people mounted 28 cameras after a promise of local control over its data. In six months the local department filed about 5,000 queries, and a public records request surfaced 1.66 million outside queries from 469 other agencies. The town now uninstalls the cameras.</li> <li><strong>Knox County, Tennessee.</strong> A 140-camera contract ended this week by unanimous commissioner vote. A deputy signed the $274,000 deal through installment orders of $24,990 each, ten dollars below the threshold requiring a commission vote. The deputy and ten colleagues face an indictment over roughly $300,000 in spending the video notes is separate from the camera system.</li> <li><strong>Chicago, Illinois.</strong> Years earlier a council member faced charges over a $130 million red-light camera deal with Redflex. The contract ended, yet the cameras stayed mounted and restarted under a new vendor without a missed day of service.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Demos run on live data.</strong> The video reports Flock sales teams demonstrated the platform using real private records, not simulated ones. Their example searches read as a profiling tool: a vehicle with a political sticker, a truck with a Trump flag, a person wearing a mask, a person holding a weapon. A list of everyone holding a weapon in an open-carry state is not a suspect list. It is pre-crime demographic profiling.</p> <hr> <h2 id="not-about-the-camera-company"> <a href="#not-about-the-camera-company" title="Not About the Camera Company">Not About the Camera Company</a> <a href="#not-about-the-camera-company" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Not About the Camera Company">#</a> </h2> <p>Focusing on one brand misses the larger fight. The video points to Axon, which sat among Flock’s early investors, shared software and data, and integrated Flock’s feed into its evidence.com platform. Red-light camera hardware in Chicago outlived its vendor and kept running under a new name. When one company falls, the sensors and the database stay behind for the next owner.</p> <p><strong>The defining trait is the sales pitch, not the sensor.</strong> Any company selling warrantless access to a comprehensive record of private movement repeats the same offense, whether the sensor is a camera, a phone, or something not yet invented.</p> <p>The two things worth defending stay fixed: the limits on government written into the Bill of Rights, and the separation of powers keeping jurisdictions apart. Mass surveillance erodes the first, and the loophole dissolves the second. Oppose the loophole wherever its sales pitch appears.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="follow" alt="simeononsecurity" > <button class="markdown-button"> Read the Detection Arms-Race Write-Up </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <hr> <h2 id="后续步骤"> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" title="后续步骤">后续步骤</a> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="后续步骤">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with the sales pitch, then move to the technical and protective sides.</p> <ul> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Camera Detection Arms Race: What Changed in 2026"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Camera Detection Arms Race: What Changed in 2026</a> </span> </strong> for the technical side of the same fight.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Cameras: Public Safety Tool or Warrantless Surveillance Machine?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-cameras-public-safety-or-surveillance-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-cameras-public-safety-or-surveillance-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Cameras: Public Safety Tool or Warrantless Surveillance Machine?</a> </span> </strong> for the surveillance framing.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Safety Camera Surveillance: Privacy and Protection"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-safety-camera-surveillance-prevalence-privacy-protection-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-safety-camera-surveillance-prevalence-privacy-protection-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Safety Camera Surveillance: Privacy and Protection</a> </span> </strong> for how the cameras spread and what protection does.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock-You Detection: Counter-Surveillance Setup Guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock-You Detection: Counter-Surveillance Setup Guide</a> </span> </strong> for building your own detector.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Source material:</strong> the argument, figures, and quotations follow <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?</a> </span> from the T-Rex Lab channel. The Fourth Amendment text comes from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Legal Information Institute"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/fourth_amendment"> <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/fourth_amendment" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Legal Information Institute</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: GrapheneOS Sandboxed Google Play Explained
item.category: "Privacy" , "Mobile Security" , "Open Source"
item.description: Learn what sandboxed Google Play changes on GrapheneOS, when a separate profile helps, and how accounts, notifications, and app compatibility fit together.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Sandboxed Google Play</strong> lets you install official Google Play components on GrapheneOS as ordinary apps. They run without the system privileges Google Play normally receives on the stock OS. Installing them is optional. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS feature overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS feature overview</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="要点"> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" title="要点">要点</a> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="要点">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain isolation:</strong> distinguish app permissions from online account activity.</li> <li><strong>Place dependencies:</strong> keep a dependent app and Play in the same profile.</li> <li><strong>Test behavior:</strong> check background notifications and essential workflows.</li> <li><strong>Build a plan:</strong> record your chosen profiles, accounts, and app requirements.</li> </ul> <h2 id="开始之前"> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" title="开始之前">开始之前</a> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="开始之前">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Audience:</strong> GrapheneOS users deciding whether to install Google Play and where to put it. <strong>Prerequisites:</strong> a supported device with an updated GrapheneOS installation and access to your essential accounts. OS installation belongs in the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/" rel="follow me" >GrapheneOS installation guide</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> 20–30 minutes for the initial app inventory and checks, plus normal daily use to assess notification reliability. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> beginner. Start with one representative app before reorganizing your phone.</p> <h2 id="what-the-sandbox-changes"> <a href="#what-the-sandbox-changes" title="What the Sandbox Changes">What the Sandbox Changes</a> <a href="#what-the-sandbox-changes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Sandbox Changes">#</a> </h2> <p>Android’s <strong>application sandbox</strong> separates app resources using operating-system protections. An app does not receive unrestricted access to another app’s private files. The protection applies to native code as well as code running through Android’s managed runtime. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Android application sandbox documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://source.android.com/docs/security/app-sandbox"> <a href="https://source.android.com/docs/security/app-sandbox" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Android application sandbox documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p>GrapheneOS adds a <strong>compatibility layer</strong> so official Play components function within those ordinary restrictions. Apps in the same profile still have supported ways to communicate by mutual consent. Sandboxing limits privileges, but it does not prevent every intentional exchange between apps. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Sandboxed Google Play design"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Sandboxed Google Play design</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Concern</th> <th>Practical meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Private app files</strong></td> <td>Installing Play does not grant unrestricted access to other apps’ data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Permissions</strong></td> <td>Review requested access as you would for another app</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Google-backed features</strong></td> <td>An app choosing a Google service still communicates with it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Account activity</strong></td> <td>Signing into a service remains a separate privacy decision</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Sandboxing and account privacy</strong> answer different questions. A sandbox restricts local access. It does not erase information you deliberately submit to an online service. For example, signing into a shopping app still identifies your account to its operator.</p> <h2 id="separate-three-privacy-decisions"> <a href="#separate-three-privacy-decisions" title="Separate Three Privacy Decisions">Separate Three Privacy Decisions</a> <a href="#separate-three-privacy-decisions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Separate Three Privacy Decisions">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Local access, service use, and identity</strong> are separate questions. For an app requesting contact access and account sign-in, review each request independently:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Decision</th> <th>Question to answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Local permission</strong></td> <td>Does this feature need my contacts, microphone, or location?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service dependency</strong></td> <td>Which feature relies on Play services?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Online identity</strong></td> <td>Which account am I associating with this activity?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A practical example:</strong> a shopping account already contains your delivery address. Moving its app into another profile does not change the address held by the retailer. Declining contact access answers a different question about data available on your phone.</p> <p><strong>Privacy objective:</strong> write the specific exposure you want to reduce. “Keep this app away from my personal contacts” is testable. “Make this account anonymous” requires decisions beyond profile placement.</p> <h2 id="owner-profile-or-separate-profile"> <a href="#owner-profile-or-separate-profile" title="Owner Profile or Separate Profile?">Owner Profile or Separate Profile?</a> <a href="#owner-profile-or-separate-profile" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Owner Profile or Separate Profile?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Owner-profile installation</strong> is a supported, straightforward choice. Google Play remains sandboxed there. A separate user or work profile helps you choose which group of apps has Play available. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS installation guidance</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Your priority</th> <th>Starting arrangement</th> <th>Tradeoff</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Simple daily use</strong></td> <td>Keep required apps and Play in Owner</td> <td>Play is available to cooperating apps in this profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Separate Google-dependent apps</strong></td> <td>Install them together in another profile</td> <td>More profile management</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Avoid Google services</strong></td> <td>Start without Play</td> <td>Check each app’s dependencies</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Profile placement</strong> matters more than installing the same component everywhere. GrapheneOS’s FAQ explains how Play availability is scoped to selected profiles, while many apps work without it or need it for only part of their functionality. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Google services FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#google-services"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#google-services" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Google services FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><em>Use a separate profile when selective Play availability solves a specific requirement you have identified.</em></p> <h2 id="understand-profile-activity"> <a href="#understand-profile-activity" title="Understand Profile Activity">Understand Profile Activity</a> <a href="#understand-profile-activity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Understand Profile Activity">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A secondary user profile</strong> has its own app instances and data. Switching to another user and ending the previous user’s session are different actions. <strong>End session</strong> stops apps in the secondary profile and returns its encrypted storage to rest. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS encryption and profile FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#encryption"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#encryption" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS encryption and profile FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Notification forwarding</strong> optionally surfaces notifications from a user running in the background to the active user. It does not keep an ended session running. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS user-profile features"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS user-profile features</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Profile state</th> <th>Delivery condition</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Active</strong></td> <td>Test delivery inside this profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Running in background</strong></td> <td>Check forwarding to the active user</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Session ended</strong></td> <td>Apps in this profile are stopped</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>For <strong>a daily messaging app</strong>, decide whether receiving messages while using Owner is essential. A profile arrangement demanding frequent session shutdown conflicts with continuous background delivery. Make this tradeoff before moving your main conversation history.</p> <h2 id="installation-and-accounts"> <a href="#installation-and-accounts" title="Installation and Accounts">Installation and Accounts</a> <a href="#installation-and-accounts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Installation and Accounts">#</a> </h2> <p>Open the built-in <strong>GrapheneOS App Store</strong>, select <strong>Google Play services</strong>, and install it. This also installs the dependent Play Store. Let the App Store maintain these components. Grant Play services a battery optimization exception for reliable background features such as push notifications. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Official installation instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Official installation instructions</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Google account sign-in</strong> is optional for functionality without an account dependency. Installing apps through the Play Store requires sign-in. Older installations also include Google Services Framework, which the project says to retain. Follow current installation instructions instead of an old three-package checklist.</p> <h2 id="test-one-app-first"> <a href="#test-one-app-first" title="Test One App First">Test One App First</a> <a href="#test-one-app-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test One App First">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a <strong>low-risk representative app</strong> to check your intended profile arrangement. Keep existing account recovery methods available throughout the exercise.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Select a profile:</strong> decide where the app belongs before installing its dependencies.</li> <li><strong>Install Play:</strong> use the official installation steps above within this profile.</li> <li><strong>Install the app:</strong> use its trusted distribution source and complete initial setup.</li> <li><strong>Review requests:</strong> approve permissions according to the feature you are testing.</li> <li><strong>Exercise one feature:</strong> send a message, open a map, or perform another reversible action.</li> <li><strong>Record the result:</strong> note the app version, OS version, profile, and exact operation.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Expected evidence:</strong> a repeatable description such as “a test message arrived with the screen locked in the active profile.” Avoid recording only “works,” which hides the feature and conditions tested.</p> <h2 id="diagnose-missing-notifications"> <a href="#diagnose-missing-notifications" title="Diagnose Missing Notifications">Diagnose Missing Notifications</a> <a href="#diagnose-missing-notifications" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Diagnose Missing Notifications">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Push notifications</strong> depend on the app’s implementation. Some apps maintain their own background connection. Others rely on Google’s Firebase Cloud Messaging. An app opening successfully does not prove its notifications work after you lock the phone. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS notification FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#notifications"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#notifications" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS notification FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Check the delivery conditions</strong> before changing permissions across several apps:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Narrow the investigation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messages appear only after opening</strong></td> <td>Check the app’s background delivery method and battery settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery works only in its profile</strong></td> <td>Check profile activity and notification forwarding</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No delivery after End session</strong></td> <td>Start the secondary profile before testing again</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>The notification arrives silently</strong></td> <td>Inspect the app’s notification channel and sound settings</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Notification channels</strong> group an app’s notification behavior, including importance and sound. Android exposes channel controls to the user. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Android notification-channel documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/notifications/channels"> <a href="https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/notifications/channels" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Android notification-channel documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Retest one condition at a time:</strong> keep the sending device and message type fixed while changing the receiving profile’s state. Record “active,” “running in background,” or “session ended” alongside each result. This distinguishes a profile-lifecycle problem from a notification configuration problem.</p> <h2 id="evaluate-essential-workflows"> <a href="#evaluate-essential-workflows" title="Evaluate Essential Workflows">Evaluate Essential Workflows</a> <a href="#evaluate-essential-workflows" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluate Essential Workflows">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a short <strong>personal acceptance test</strong> before relying on a new setup:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Workflow</th> <th>Check on your device</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messaging</strong></td> <td>Receive a message with the screen locked</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Account access</strong></td> <td>Sign in and complete the required second factor</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Banking or payments</strong></td> <td>Test the exact function you need, including any device checks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Navigation</strong></td> <td>Obtain location with your chosen permissions</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An app launching</strong> is only the first check. Record the app version, GrapheneOS version, and failed operation when troubleshooting. This article provides a decision framework, not a tested compatibility list.</p> <p><strong>Migration decision:</strong> keep your previous access method until each essential operation has passed. A messaging app and a banking app need different acceptance criteria. Successful message delivery says nothing about another app’s account or device checks.</p> <p><strong>Recheck after GrapheneOS or app updates.</strong> Profile placement, permissions, notification channels, and session state still define the test. Record the version beside each result so a changed notification or sign-in behavior does not become an unexplained privacy conclusion.</p> <p>For <strong>a work login</strong>, test the complete sign-in sequence and the required second factor. For a travel app, test the feature you expect to use away from home. Choose representative actions without making unnecessary purchases or changing account security.</p> <h2 id="build-your-app-plan"> <a href="#build-your-app-plan" title="Build Your App Plan">Build Your App Plan</a> <a href="#build-your-app-plan" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build Your App Plan">#</a> </h2> <p>Complete this <strong>inventory</strong> for your five most important apps. The rows below are prompts, not compatibility claims about specific products:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>App category</th> <th>Requirement to record</th> <th>Evidence to collect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messaging</strong></td> <td>Background delivery and profile choice</td> <td>Locked-screen and background-profile test</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Work access</strong></td> <td>Required login and second factor</td> <td>Completed sign-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Navigation</strong></td> <td>Location permission and offline needs</td> <td>A route under expected conditions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Banking</strong></td> <td>Essential supported operations</td> <td>Results for each required function</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Shopping</strong></td> <td>Account and local-data access</td> <td>Permission review and normal account use</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Write a decision</strong> for each row: chosen profile, Play dependency, account requirement, approved permissions, and fallback. Leave unknown dependencies marked unknown until you have evidence. This avoids installing additional components merely because another app needed them.</p> <p><strong>Review exercise:</strong> an app works while its secondary profile is active, then stops receiving messages after End session. The first action is to restart the profile and retest. Granting contact access would not address a stopped session.</p> <p><strong>Completion criterion:</strong> your plan should explain why each app sits in its chosen profile and which test supports relying on it. Revisit the relevant row after an update changes behavior.</p> <h2 id="后续步骤"> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" title="后续步骤">后续步骤</a> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="后续步骤">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/" rel="follow me" >GrapheneOS installation guide</a> </span> if you have not installed the OS. Then choose one profile arrangement and test your essential apps before adding extra profiles or changing broad permission settings.</p> Read More at https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Microsoft SOC Home Lab: Build Cybersecurity Experience in 2026
item.category: "Cybersecurity" , "Cloud Security" , "Career Development"
item.description: Build a Microsoft SOC home lab with Sentinel, Defender, Intune, and Entra. Practice incident investigation, validate passkey policies, and document portfolio evidence.
item.content:encoded: <p>A <strong>security operations center (SOC) home lab</strong> gives you a place to investigate alerts, explain evidence, and test defensive changes. Build a small Microsoft environment, collect its telemetry, and write up each investigation. The useful result is a repeatable investigation with supporting evidence.</p> <p>This guide develops the lab approach described in Mad Hat’s cybersecurity career video and supplied Cyber Range runbook. It uses Microsoft documentation for product requirements and separates setup, detection, and validation into measurable tasks.</p> <h2 id="要点"> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" title="要点">要点</a> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="要点">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Start small:</strong> one managed Windows client and one test identity support the first exercises.</li> <li><strong>Verify telemetry:</strong> a visible device or connected portal does not prove logs are arriving.</li> <li><strong>Complete the investigation:</strong> record the trigger, evidence, response, and retest.</li> <li><strong>Control spending:</strong> track licenses, retained data, networking, and compute separately.</li> <li><strong>Describe experience accurately:</strong> list the environment as a lab project on your resume.</li> </ul> <h2 id="开始之前"> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" title="开始之前">开始之前</a> <a href="#%e5%bc%80%e5%a7%8b%e4%b9%8b%e5%89%8d" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="开始之前">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> basic Windows administration, networking, and familiarity with virtual machines. Use a dedicated Microsoft Entra tenant and an Azure subscription reserved for the lab. Keep production identities, personal files, and employer systems outside the exercise.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> allow a weekend for the initial setup, followed by focused investigation sessions. This is a planning estimate. Trial approval, quota availability, and service provisioning affect elapsed time. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> intermediate.</p> <p>Prepare a separate administrative account and an unprivileged test user. Before testing access policies, establish and verify emergency access. Assign privileges for each setup task, then use a lower-privilege account for routine investigation.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>Lab purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Sentinel</strong></td> <td>Security information and event management, or SIEM, for connected log sources</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender XDR</strong></td> <td>Correlation and investigation across licensed Microsoft security services</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender for Endpoint</strong></td> <td>Endpoint detection and response, or EDR, on onboarded devices</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Intune</strong></td> <td>Device enrollment and endpoint security policy management</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Entra ID</strong></td> <td>Identity, sign-in records, and access policy evaluation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender for Servers</strong></td> <td>Server protection through Defender for Cloud</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="check-licenses-first"> <a href="#check-licenses-first" title="Check Licenses First">Check Licenses First</a> <a href="#check-licenses-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Licenses First">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Microsoft 365 E5</strong> is one route to a broad lab, but access depends on the service plans and licenses assigned to the participating users. Office 365 E5 and Microsoft 365 E5 are different bundles. A single administrator’s license does not establish coverage for every test user or workload. Review the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Defender XDR prerequisites"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/prerequisites"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/prerequisites" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Defender XDR prerequisites</a> </span> before selecting a subscription.</p> <p><strong>Sentinel in the Defender portal</strong> works without E5 or Defender XDR. Adding XDR introduces its own licensing and configuration requirements. An empty incident view is not evidence of missing E5 licensing. Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Sentinel onboarding documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Sentinel onboarding documentation</a> </span> explains both configurations.</p> <p><strong>Server protection</strong> has a separate licensing path. Defender for Servers integrates with Defender for Endpoint for supported server workloads. Windows client operating systems need appropriate client coverage. Do not treat every Azure VM as an automatically licensed server. See Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Defender for Endpoint integration documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Defender for Endpoint integration documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Trial planning:</strong> confirm eligibility, expiration, renewal settings, and included services in your own account. Avoid budgeting around a promised trial duration or a fixed monthly total from a video.</p> <h2 id="set-a-spending-plan"> <a href="#set-a-spending-plan" title="Set a Spending Plan">Set a Spending Plan</a> <a href="#set-a-spending-plan" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set a Spending Plan">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Azure budgets</strong> send notifications. They do not stop consumption when you reach a threshold. Cost reporting also has a delay. Create alerts early and review spending after each session, following Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="budget setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >budget setup guide</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Cost category</th> <th>Planning question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>User licenses</strong></td> <td>Which users need which service plans, and when do trials expire?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Compute</strong></td> <td>How many VM hours will each exercise require?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storage</strong></td> <td>Which disks and snapshots remain after shutdown?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Log collection</strong></td> <td>Which tables need ingestion and how long should data remain?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Networking</strong></td> <td>Does the design include paid Bastion, public IPs, or outbound services?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Server protection</strong></td> <td>Which workloads have a paid Defender plan enabled?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Design choice:</strong> begin with one client. Add a server when an exercise needs server telemetry. Four clients and several servers add administration and cost before they add useful investigation practice.</p> <h2 id="build-the-network"> <a href="#build-the-network" title="Build the Network">Build the Network</a> <a href="#build-the-network" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build the Network">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Suggested layout:</strong> put Azure resources in a clearly named group such as <strong><code>rg-soc-lab</code></strong>. Use separate client and server subnets, explicit network security group rules, and private management access. Subnet separation alone does not block traffic between workloads.</p> <p>For a dedicated <strong>Azure Bastion</strong> deployment, follow the SKU requirements, including the reserved <strong><code>AzureBastionSubnet</code></strong> name and a <strong><code>/26</code></strong> or larger subnet for current deployments. Developer SKU uses a different deployment model. Review <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bastion configuration settings"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/configuration-settings"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/configuration-settings" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Bastion configuration settings</a> </span> before choosing a design.</p> <p>Keep RDP and SSH closed to the public internet. Restrict management traffic to the selected management path. Allow the outbound service connectivity needed for enrollment and security telemetry.</p> <p><strong>Validation:</strong> establish private management access and verify effective network rules before installing workloads. If you add a deliberately vulnerable application later, keep it inside the exercise network and restrict access to the test machines.</p> <h2 id="connect-sentinel-and-logs"> <a href="#connect-sentinel-and-logs" title="Connect Sentinel and Logs">Connect Sentinel and Logs</a> <a href="#connect-sentinel-and-logs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Connect Sentinel and Logs">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Portal setup:</strong> create a Log Analytics workspace and enable Sentinel on it. If the workspace is absent from the Defender portal, open <strong>System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Connect a workspace</strong>. Verify the tenant and required Azure and Entra roles against the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="onboarding prerequisites"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >onboarding prerequisites</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Log collection is a separate step.</strong> In Entra, configure diagnostic settings to send the required activity categories to the same workspace. Start with interactive sign-ins and audit events. Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Entra log integration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-integrate-activity-logs-with-azure-monitor-logs"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-integrate-activity-logs-with-azure-monitor-logs" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Entra log integration guide</a> </span> covers the permissions and destination setup.</p> <p>The current Sentinel workflow also supports connection through the Microsoft Defender portal. Confirm the workspace is the intended primary workspace, the tenant matches the test identities, and the account has the required roles before troubleshooting an empty table. Portal visibility alone does not prove ingestion. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Sentinel onboarding in the Defender portal"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/microsoft-sentinel-onboard"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/microsoft-sentinel-onboard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Sentinel onboarding in the Defender portal</a> </span> </p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-kusto" data-lang="kusto">SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where UserPrincipalName =~ "soc-test@YOUR-TENANT.onmicrosoft.com" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus, CorrelationId | order by TimeGenerated desc </code></pre><p>Run this <strong>Kusto Query Language (KQL)</strong> example in the workspace’s Logs view after generating a fresh test sign-in. Replace the sample user principal name with your lab user. The columns follow the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SigninLogs table schema"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/signinlogs"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/signinlogs" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SigninLogs table schema</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Expected result:</strong> a row matching the test account and sign-in time. No rows means you need to check the time range, identity, collection settings, destination, and ingestion delay. A missing table points to a collection or workspace issue before it points to a detection issue.</p> <h2 id="onboard-the-first-endpoint"> <a href="#onboard-the-first-endpoint" title="Onboard the First Endpoint">Onboard the First Endpoint</a> <a href="#onboard-the-first-endpoint" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Onboard the First Endpoint">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Intune enrollment and EDR onboarding</strong> are separate checkpoints. Connect Intune and Defender for Endpoint, enroll a supported Windows client, then assign an endpoint detection and response onboarding policy to its lab group. Entra registration alone does not establish either checkpoint.</p> <p>In Intune, check <strong>Endpoint security > Defender for Endpoint</strong>. If the connection is unavailable, enable the Intune connection in Defender’s endpoint advanced features. Follow the platform-specific steps in Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Intune and Defender integration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/microsoft-defender/configure-integration"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/microsoft-defender/configure-integration" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Intune and Defender integration guide</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Checkpoint</th> <th>Evidence to capture</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Enrollment</strong></td> <td>Client appears in Intune with a recent check-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Policy assignment</strong></td> <td>Onboarding policy applies to the intended device group</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sensor reporting</strong></td> <td>Defender shows onboarded status and recent telemetry</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Detection test</strong></td> <td>A documented test produces the expected security signal</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>For servers</strong>, enable the chosen Defender for Servers plan and its endpoint integration, then verify sensor deployment and reporting. Defender for Cloud also discovers machines before onboarding completes. Inventory presence alone is insufficient, as Microsoft explains in its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="resource discovery and onboarding guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >resource discovery and onboarding guidance</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="investigate-a-test-alert"> <a href="#investigate-a-test-alert" title="Investigate a Test Alert">Investigate a Test Alert</a> <a href="#investigate-a-test-alert" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Investigate a Test Alert">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start with Microsoft’s documented EDR detection test</strong> on the lab endpoint. Follow the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="current test instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-detection"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-detection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >current test instructions</a> </span> , including platform prerequisites and troubleshooting. Record the execution time before opening the alert queue.</p> <p>Treat the resulting alert as an investigation exercise. A security product’s title gives you a starting point. Your job is to establish what happened and support the disposition with evidence.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Triage:</strong> identify the alert source, device, account, and event time.</li> <li><strong>Inspect:</strong> review the process tree, command line, file details, and network activity available for the event.</li> <li><strong>Scope:</strong> search for related activity on the test identity and other lab devices.</li> <li><strong>Assess:</strong> explain whether the evidence matches the planned exercise or an unrelated event.</li> <li><strong>Respond:</strong> document the selected response, its impact, and the recovery steps. Perform supported containment only when the exercise requires it.</li> <li><strong>Retest:</strong> repeat the relevant test after changing a control and compare the evidence.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Do not manufacture missing results.</strong> If the alert fails to arrive, preserve the execution record and troubleshoot collection. If a control blocks the test before the expected event, document the prevention result.</p> <h2 id="test-identity-controls"> <a href="#test-identity-controls" title="Test Identity Controls">Test Identity Controls</a> <a href="#test-identity-controls" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test Identity Controls">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing</strong> places an attacker-controlled intermediary in a sign-in flow. The supplied runbook uses this scenario to motivate stronger authentication. For the first identity exercise, test policy behavior directly with your own unprivileged account.</p> <p>Begin by recording a legitimate sign-in and its authentication details. Review Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Entra risk detection reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Entra risk detection reference</a> </span> before interpreting risk signals. Detection prerequisites and processing differ by signal. A new IP address or a failed sign-in does not guarantee an AiTM alert.</p> <p><strong>Passkeys (FIDO2)</strong> use credentials bound to the legitimate service rather than reusable codes entered into a relayed login page. Enable an appropriate passkey profile for the pilot group and register the method before enforcing a policy. Follow Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="passkey configuration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >passkey configuration guide</a> </span> for supported authenticators and restrictions.</p> <p><strong>Conditional Access exercise:</strong> create a policy targeting only the lab pilot group, exclude emergency access accounts, and select <strong>Require authentication strength > Phishing-resistant MFA strength</strong>. Start in <strong>Report-only</strong>, review its impact, then enable it. This adapts Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="administrator policy example"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-admin-phish-resistant-mfa"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-admin-phish-resistant-mfa" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >administrator policy example</a> </span> to a narrow test group.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Evidence to collect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Report-only policy</strong></td> <td>Sign-in record showing how the proposed policy evaluates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Enforced policy, weaker method</strong></td> <td>Fresh authentication requires a stronger method before access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Enforced policy, registered passkey</strong></td> <td>Successful sign-in satisfying the required strength</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Use fresh authentication for each comparison and inspect the policy details. Existing sessions complicate comparisons. <strong>Scope of proof:</strong> this exercise validates the authentication requirement. It does not demonstrate universal protection against endpoint compromise or theft of an existing session.</p> <h2 id="write-portfolio-evidence"> <a href="#write-portfolio-evidence" title="Write Portfolio Evidence">Write Portfolio Evidence</a> <a href="#write-portfolio-evidence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Write Portfolio Evidence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A useful portfolio entry</strong> explains a decision another analyst is able to review. Include a short architecture description, the collection prerequisites, the event timeline, and the reasoning behind your response.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Exercise: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Date and UTC time window: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Lab scope and prerequisites: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Trigger and expected signal: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observed alert or prevention: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Evidence and queries: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Affected identities and devices: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Disposition and reasoning: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Response and recovery: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Control change and retest: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Limitations and follow-up: </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Replace every field with your own observations. <strong>Sanitize exports:</strong> remove credentials, session material, personal information, and unnecessary identifiers before publishing screenshots or query results.</p> <p><strong>Resume example:</strong> “Built a Microsoft security lab, connected identity logs to Sentinel, investigated endpoint test alerts, and documented Conditional Access validation.” Use this wording only after completing those tasks. Put it under projects or practical training with the actual dates and scope.</p> <p>A lab demonstrates independent practice. <strong>Production SOC work</strong> also involves business impact, escalation, service commitments, and coordination with other teams. Explain which parts you practiced and which remain outside your experience.</p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>First check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Workspace absent from Defender</strong></td> <td>Same tenant, Sentinel enabled, and onboarding role requirements</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SigninLogs absent or empty</strong></td> <td>Diagnostic categories, destination workspace, fresh events, and time range</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Client absent from Intune</strong></td> <td>Enrollment prerequisites and enrollment status</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Device visible without telemetry</strong></td> <td>Actual onboarding state, sensor health, and outbound connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Onboarding policy unapplied</strong></td> <td>Assignment scope, device platform, and recent check-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No identity risk alert</strong></td> <td>Signal prerequisites and recorded activity, without assuming deterministic detection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected access allowed</strong></td> <td>Report-only status, exclusions, resource scope, and existing session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Charges after shutdown</strong></td> <td>Allocation state and resources billed independently of compute</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Troubleshooting order:</strong> prove the event happened, prove collection worked, then investigate detection logic. Record each failure and fix in the project notes.</p> <h2 id="pause-or-remove-the-lab"> <a href="#pause-or-remove-the-lab" title="Pause or Remove the Lab">Pause or Remove the Lab</a> <a href="#pause-or-remove-the-lab" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pause or Remove the Lab">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Deallocation</strong> releases VM compute allocation. A guest operating system shutdown alone does not guarantee deallocation. Check Azure’s displayed power state and review Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="VM states and billing documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/states-billing"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/states-billing" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >VM states and billing documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Retained resources</strong> still need review. Disks, snapshots, networking services, log retention, and user subscriptions have separate lifecycles. Set a reminder before each trial expires and verify the next usage report after cleanup.</p> <p>Before deleting the lab resource group, export the evidence you intend to retain and inspect its contents. <strong>Resource group deletion is destructive</strong> for contained resources. Tenant users, Intune policies, Conditional Access policies, subscriptions, and subscription-level security settings require separate cleanup where applicable.</p> <h2 id="后续步骤"> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" title="后续步骤">后续步骤</a> <a href="#%e5%90%8e%e7%bb%ad%e6%ad%a5%e9%aa%a4" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="后续步骤">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Finish one documented investigation</strong> before adding another workload. Then add a server, an identity exercise, or a detection rule with a clear test condition. Track what the added component teaches and what it costs.</p> <p>Use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT home lab guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/" rel="follow me" >IT home lab guide</a> </span> for infrastructure practice and the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT resume guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/" rel="follow me" >IT resume guide</a> </span> to present the work. Keep the next project small enough to explain from setup through evidence and cleanup.</p> Read More at https://zh.simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: The Most Common Types of Cyberattacks and How Defenders Catch Them
item.category: "Cybersecurity" , "Threat Detection" , "Blue Team" , "Security Operations" , "Career Development"
item.description: A practical tour of the most common cyberattack types, the evidence each one leaves behind in logs and telemetry, and how to practice detecting them in a home security lab.
item.content:encoded: <p>An <strong>attack type</strong> is a category of technique, not a single tool. Ransomware, phishing, and credential stuffing each name a method an adversary repeats against many targets with minor variations. Learning the categories gives you a mental index for the alerts you will meet on a security team.</p> <p><em>Individual malware families appear and disappear within months. The attack categories below have stayed stable for years, and each one leaves a recognizable trail in endpoint, identity, network, or email telemetry.</em></p> <h2 id="要点"> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" title="要点">要点</a> <a href="#%e8%a6%81%e7%82%b9" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="要点">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Learn the pattern, not the payload.</strong> Attack categories change far slower than individual tools.</li> <li><strong>Every category leaves evidence.</strong> The detection work starts with knowing which telemetry records the activity.</li> <li><strong>Reproduce an attack to understand it.</strong> A home lab turns an abstract category into a recorded observation.</li> <li><strong>Write up what you found.</strong> A short investigation note proves the work and teaches you the evidence.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-attack-types-at-a-glance"> <a href="#the-attack-types-at-a-glance" title="The Attack Types at a Glance">The Attack Types at a Glance</a> <a href="#the-attack-types-at-a-glance" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Attack Types at a Glance">#</a> </h2> <p>The table below lists the categories security teams meet most often. Each later section describes the category, its common variants, and the data a defender reviews to find it.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack type</th> <th>What it does</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Malware</strong></td> <td>Runs malicious software such as ransomware, spyware, and trojans</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Denial of service</strong></td> <td>Floods a service with traffic until legitimate users lose access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Phishing</strong></td> <td>Tricks a person into revealing credentials or running a malicious file</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spoofing</strong></td> <td>Disguises an attacker as a trusted system, sender, or address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity-based attacks</strong></td> <td>Abuses stolen or forged credentials to act as a valid user</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Code injection</strong></td> <td>Inserts malicious code into an application to change its behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Supply chain attacks</strong></td> <td>Compromises a trusted vendor, library, or update channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Social engineering</strong></td> <td>Manipulates a person into taking an unsafe action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Insider threats</strong></td> <td>Misuses access held by a current or former employee</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS tunneling</strong></td> <td>Encodes data inside DNS queries to move it past controls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IoT attacks</strong></td> <td>Targets connected devices to pivot, spy, or join a botnet</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AI-powered attacks</strong></td> <td>Uses machine learning to generate content, impersonate people, or evade filters</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A note on scope:</strong> these categories overlap. A phishing email often delivers malware, and a successful credential theft often precedes an identity-based attack. Treat the list as a set of lenses rather than rigid boxes.</p> <hr> <h2 id="malware"> <a href="#malware" title="Malware">Malware</a> <a href="#malware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Malware">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Malware</strong> covers any program built to harm, control, or profit from a system. The term spans ransomware, fileless malware, spyware, adware, trojans, worms, rootkits, keyloggers, and botnets.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Subtype</th> <th>Behavior</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Ransomware</strong></td> <td>Encrypts files and demands payment for the decryption key</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fileless malware</strong></td> <td>Runs through built-in system tools and writes little to disk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spyware</strong></td> <td>Collects activity data without the user’s knowledge</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Trojan</strong></td> <td>Poses as legitimate software to gain execution</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Worm</strong></td> <td>Copies itself across hosts without user action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Rootkit</strong></td> <td>Hides inside the operating system to keep persistent control</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> endpoint detection and response tools, or <strong>EDR</strong>, record process trees, command lines, file writes, and registry changes. Even a fileless attack produces process and script-block telemetry, because the operating system still launches the tools it abuses.</p> <hr> <h2 id="denial-of-service"> <a href="#denial-of-service" title="Denial of Service">Denial of Service</a> <a href="#denial-of-service" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Denial of Service">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A denial-of-service (DoS) attack</strong> floods a target with requests until legitimate users lose access. <strong>A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack</strong> repeats the same idea from many systems at once, which makes the traffic far harder to filter by source address.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Trait</th> <th>DoS</th> <th>DDoS</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Origin</strong></td> <td>One system</td> <td>Many systems</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Blocking difficulty</strong></td> <td>Moderate</td> <td>High, since the sources span many networks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Typical impact</strong></td> <td>Lost availability</td> <td>Lost availability at larger scale</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> traffic volume against a baseline, connection counts per source, request-rate spikes, and error-rate changes. Availability monitoring often alerts before the security team sees the event.</p> <hr> <h2 id="phishing"> <a href="#phishing" title="Phishing">Phishing</a> <a href="#phishing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Phishing">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Phishing</strong> uses email, text messages, phone calls, or social media to push a person toward revealing credentials or running a malicious attachment. The category splits by target and channel.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Variant</th> <th>Target and channel</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Spear phishing</strong></td> <td>A specific person or team, usually by email</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Whaling</strong></td> <td>Senior or executive staff, often to move money or data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Smishing</strong></td> <td>Fraudulent text messages</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vishing</strong></td> <td>Fraudulent phone calls or voice messages</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> mail-gateway logs, URL detonation results, attachment analysis, and user reports. A report from a cautious employee is one of the highest-value signals on this list.</p> <hr> <h2 id="spoofing"> <a href="#spoofing" title="Spoofing">Spoofing</a> <a href="#spoofing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Spoofing">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Spoofing</strong> hides an attacker behind a trusted identity so a target accepts the connection, message, or address. The disguise buys time and defeats checks built around trust.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>What gets faked</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Domain spoofing</strong></td> <td>A lookalike website or email domain impersonating a real brand</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Email spoofing</strong></td> <td>The sender address on a message</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ARP spoofing</strong></td> <td>A local network address, to intercept traffic between two hosts</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results in mail headers, domain registration age, certificate mismatches, and duplicate address warnings on a local network.</p> <hr> <h2 id="identity-based-attacks"> <a href="#identity-based-attacks" title="Identity-Based Attacks">Identity-Based Attacks</a> <a href="#identity-based-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Identity-Based Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Identity-based attacks</strong> use a valid account rather than a defect in software. The attacker holds a working credential, so the activity sits close to normal use and blends into the background. This category drives a large share of the alerts a <strong>security operations center (SOC)</strong> handles each day.</p> <p><em>If you practice one category in a home lab, choose this one. The signals are rich, the exercises repeat, and the setup stays small.</em></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>What happens</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Kerberoasting</strong></td> <td>Requests a service ticket, then cracks the encrypted password offline</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Man-in-the-middle (MITM)</strong></td> <td>Sits between two parties to read or alter a session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Pass-the-hash</strong></td> <td>Reuses a stolen password hash to open a new session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Golden ticket</strong></td> <td>Forges a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket for broad domain access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Silver ticket</strong></td> <td>Forges a service ticket for one specific service</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Credential harvesting</strong></td> <td>Collects usernames and passwords in bulk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Credential stuffing</strong></td> <td>Replays one set of credentials across many unrelated sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Password spraying</strong></td> <td>Tries one common password across many accounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Brute force</strong></td> <td>Guesses many passwords against one account</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Downgrade</strong></td> <td>Forces a connection into a weaker protocol version</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> sign-in records, failed-authentication counts, token anomalies, impossible-travel flags, and identity risk detections. <strong>Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing</strong> belongs here too, because the attacker steals a live session token rather than a password, and the replay from unfamiliar infrastructure trips the identity risk engine.</p> <hr> <h2 id="code-injection"> <a href="#code-injection" title="Code Injection">Code Injection</a> <a href="#code-injection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Code Injection">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Code injection</strong> places attacker-controlled code inside a vulnerable application so the application runs it as part of normal work. The application, not the attacker, carries out the harmful action.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>Target</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SQL injection</strong></td> <td>A database query built from unvalidated input</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cross-site scripting (XSS)</strong></td> <td>A web page which renders attacker script in a visitor’s browser</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Malvertising</strong></td> <td>A legitimate ad slot filled with malicious code</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data poisoning</strong></td> <td>A training set for an AI or machine learning model</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> web application logs, database query records, content security policy reports, and request patterns which differ from normal application use.</p> <hr> <h2 id="supply-chain-attacks"> <a href="#supply-chain-attacks" title="Supply Chain Attacks">Supply Chain Attacks</a> <a href="#supply-chain-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supply Chain Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A supply chain attack</strong> targets a trusted third party whose product or service reaches many customers. A <strong>software supply chain attack</strong> injects malicious code into an application, library, or update so every user of the product receives it. A <strong>hardware supply chain attack</strong> compromises a physical component before it ships.</p> <p><em>Modern software leans on third-party libraries, so one compromised dependency reaches far past the original vendor.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> software composition analysis, build-pipeline records, unexpected outbound connections from a trusted update, and integrity checks on shipped artifacts.</p> <hr> <h2 id="social-engineering"> <a href="#social-engineering" title="Social Engineering">Social Engineering</a> <a href="#social-engineering" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Social Engineering">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Social engineering</strong> uses psychological pressure to move a person toward an unsafe action. The attacker appeals to authority, urgency, fear, money, or trust.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>Approach</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Pretexting</strong></td> <td>Invents a believable scenario to gain trust</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Business email compromise (BEC)</strong></td> <td>Impersonates a trusted colleague to redirect a payment or share data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disinformation</strong></td> <td>Spreads false narratives through social media and bots</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Quid pro quo</strong></td> <td>Offers a reward in exchange for information or access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Honeytrap</strong></td> <td>Builds a false relationship to extract money, data, or access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tailgating</strong></td> <td>Follows an employee through a secured door</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> email authentication results, unusual payment-change requests, helpdesk records, and physical access logs.</p> <hr> <h2 id="insider-threats"> <a href="#insider-threats" title="Insider Threats">Insider Threats</a> <a href="#insider-threats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Insider Threats">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An insider threat</strong> is misuse of access by a current or former employee, contractor, or partner. Some insiders act with intent, driven by money or grievance. Others act through negligence, such as leaving credentials in a shared document.</p> <p><em>Negligent insiders appear more often than malicious ones in incident reports, and both call for the same detective control: compare access against a baseline for the role.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> data-transfer volume, activity outside normal hours, privilege changes, and bulk downloads from sensitive repositories.</p> <hr> <h2 id="dns-tunneling"> <a href="#dns-tunneling" title="DNS Tunneling">DNS Tunneling</a> <a href="#dns-tunneling" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="DNS Tunneling">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>DNS tunneling</strong> encodes data inside DNS queries and responses. Almost every network permits DNS, so the technique moves data past controls built to inspect web traffic.</p> <p><em>Detection leans on volume and shape. A single host sending thousands of queries to one domain stands apart from a normal baseline, and unusually long subdomains hint at an encoded payload.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> DNS query records, query length and volume per host, uncommon record types such as TXT, and lookups to domains registered days earlier.</p> <hr> <h2 id="iot-based-attacks"> <a href="#iot-based-attacks" title="IoT-Based Attacks">IoT-Based Attacks</a> <a href="#iot-based-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="IoT-Based Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An IoT-based attack</strong> targets a connected device such as a camera, printer, thermostat, or sensor. Weak default credentials and rare firmware updates make these devices a common foothold.
